content.title: About
content.content: Chili is a hot pepper derived from various Capsicum cultivars. The NFS (New Fresh Spice) version is a fresh, non‑dried pepper that retains maximum aroma and heat. Chili is widely used in cooking to add spiciness and is a key ingredient in sauces, marinades, and spice blends.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Capsaicin, the compound responsible for heat, also has mild analgesic properties.
Different chili varieties are measured on the Scoville scale, ranging from mild sweet (0–500) to extreme (over 1,000,000).
Chili was used in traditional medicine by ancient Mesoamerican cultures to aid digestion.
Dried chili can be stored for up to a year, while fresh NFS should be used within 7‑10 days.
In some cultures chili is considered a protective talisman against evil spirits.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and aids collagen synthesis.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Capsaicin and carotenoids protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Boosts metabolism
items.content: Capsaicin may increase calorie burning and help with weight management.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Antioxidant properties help lower LDL cholesterol levels.

items.title: Source of vitamin A
items.content: Vitamin A is essential for vision and skin health.

items.title: Stomach irritation
items.content: Consuming large amounts of hot chili can cause heartburn or gastric irritation.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to capsaicin or other pepper components.

items.title: Increased body temperature
items.content: Capsaicin triggers sweating and a feeling of heat, which may be uncomfortable with fever.

items.title: Interaction with medications
items.content: Hot peppers can enhance the effects of anticoagulants, so caution is advised for users of such drugs.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Fresh NFS chili can be thinly sliced and added to salads, soups, sauces, and marinades. It is also used to make spicy pastes, chips, and flavored oils. To reduce heat, remove the seeds and inner membrane.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh chili in the refrigerator in an airtight container for 5‑7 days. For longer preservation, freeze it in bags or dry it; dried chili keeps well in a cool, dark place for up to a year.

content.title: About
content.content: Cocoa powder is made from roasted, ground cocoa beans (Theobroma cacao) after most of the cocoa butter has been pressed out. It is a dark brown, bitter, unsweetened powder with an intense chocolate flavor. Cocoa powder is used in baking, desserts, hot cocoa, smoothies, and sauces.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Natural cocoa powder is acidic and lighter in color, while Dutch-processed (alkalized) cocoa is treated to neutralize acidity and is darker and milder.
Cocoa beans come from the seeds of the cacao tree, which is native to tropical regions of the Americas.
Cocoa naturally contains theobromine, a mild stimulant related to caffeine.
Unsweetened cocoa powder is very bitter, unlike sweetened drinking chocolate mixes.
Cocoa is rich in plant compounds called flavanols, though processing can reduce them.

items.title: Contains flavanols
items.content: Cocoa contains flavanols, plant compounds with antioxidant properties that are being studied.

items.title: Provides magnesium and iron
items.content: Cocoa provides magnesium and iron, which support muscle function and oxygen transport.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: Cocoa powder contributes fiber that supports digestion.

items.title: Provides copper and manganese
items.content: These minerals support normal metabolism.

items.title: Intense flavor with little sugar
items.content: Unsweetened cocoa adds chocolate flavor without added sugar.

items.title: Caffeine and theobromine
items.content: Cocoa contains stimulants that may cause restlessness, trouble sleeping, or a fast heartbeat in sensitive people, children, and during pregnancy if eaten in large amounts.

items.title: Heavy metals
items.content: Some cocoa products contain traces of cadmium and lead, so eat cocoa in moderation and choose reputable brands.

items.title: Toxic to dogs
items.content: Cocoa and chocolate are toxic to dogs and cats because of theobromine, so keep them away from pets.

items.title: Allergies, migraines, and added sugar
items.content: Cocoa can trigger reactions or migraines in some people, and sweetened cocoa mixes can be high in sugar.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cocoa powder can be sifted into cake, brownie, cookie, and pancake batters, stirred into oatmeal or smoothies, or whisked with hot milk and a little sweetener to make hot cocoa. Use unsweetened cocoa powder when you want to control the sugar. Dutch-processed and natural cocoa behave differently in baking recipes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cocoa powder in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place, where it keeps for a year or longer. Keep it away from moisture and strong odors. Discard cocoa that has clumped, smells musty, or shows mold.

content.title: About
content.content: Gelatin dessert with fruit is a sweet dish made from gelatin that incorporates pieces of fresh or canned fruit. The gelatin gives the dessert a light, wobbly texture, while the fruit adds natural sweetness, aroma, and a boost of vitamins.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The modern gelatin dessert became popular in Europe in the 19th century as a way to preserve fruit for longer periods.
Vegetarian and vegan alternatives to gelatin include agar‑agar and pectin.
The color of the dessert depends on the type of gelatin and the fruits used: strawberries yield a pink hue, oranges an orange tint.
Traditionally, gelatin desserts are served in small portions in cups or molded shapes.

items.title: Rich in vitamins
items.content: Fruit pieces provide vitamin C, vitamin A and B‑complex vitamins, supporting immunity and vision.

items.title: Low‑calorie dessert
items.content: Gelatin desserts are low in fat and calories, making them suitable for weight‑controlled diets.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: Because gelatin is mostly water, it helps contribute to daily fluid intake.

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: Gelatin breaks down quickly in the stomach, making the dessert gentle on the digestive system.

items.title: Gelatin allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to gelatin derived from animal collagen.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Commercially prepared versions often contain added sugar, which can be problematic for people with diabetes.

items.title: Artificial additives
items.content: Certain colorings and flavorings may cause sensitivity in susceptible individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dessert chilled; garnish with fresh berries, mint leaves, or a sprinkle of nuts. It can be eaten directly from a cup or unmolded from a silicone mold using a spoon.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared gelatin dessert in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑5 days. Over time, the flavor and texture may change.

content.title: About
content.content: Cherry strudel is a classic baked dessert made from thin pastry dough filled with a sweet cherry mixture. The dough is prepared from flour, eggs, butter and water, while the filling consists of fresh or frozen cherries, sugar and sometimes aromatic spices such as cinnamon and vanilla.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Strudel originates from Austria, where it is considered a national dish.
The cherry version became popular in Eastern Europe thanks to abundant cherry harvests.
Traditional strudel dough is rolled out to a thickness of 1–2 mm.
Original recipes often include nuts and raisins, but cherry strudel is frequently served without them.
Strudel is commonly dusted with powdered sugar or served with a butter sauce.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Cherries contain anthocyanins and vitamin C, which help combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Fiber from the cherries and whole‑grain dough promotes healthy bowel function.

items.title: Source of potassium
items.content: Potassium in cherries helps regulate blood pressure.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: When made with modest butter, the pastry contains less saturated fat than many other baked goods.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Whole‑wheat dough provides B1 and B3 vitamins important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The dough contains wheat flour, which can trigger reactions in people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: The filling is often sweetened, so those monitoring blood sugar should limit portion size.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: Butter and dough make the strudel energy‑dense; moderation is key.

items.title: Acidity of cherries
items.content: For some individuals the tartness of cherries may cause heartburn.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the strudel warm, sliced into portions. It can be dusted with powdered sugar, drizzled with butter sauce, or paired with ice cream. For a lighter version, use whole‑grain dough and reduce added sugar.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the strudel in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2 days. For longer storage, refrigerate (up to 5 days) or freeze (up to 2 months). Reheat in the oven before serving to restore a crisp crust.
